title: Twisted
full_review:
A female homicide detective with a tortured past becomes her own prime suspect in the abysmally bad neo-noir thriller "Twisted" (Paramount). Navigating a minefield of moth-eaten cop cliches and laugh-inducing dialogue with all the grace of an elephant with vertigo, Philip Kaufman has succeeded in inadvertently crafting one of the funniest movies in recent years; the only problem is it's not supposed to be a comedy.

Ashley Judd stars as recently promoted Jessica Shepard, a brassy boozer with a new gold shield and an off-duty appetite for trolling seedy bars looking for one-night stands of rough sex. When each guy she sleeps with winds up a victim in the string of serial murders she is investigating, all clues seem to point to her as the killer. Compounding the already contrived conceit, Jessica also suffers from inexplicable blackouts, raising self-doubts about her own innocence. Of course, by this time audience members may themselves wish that they could suddenly lose consciousness -- at least until the end of the movie.
Playing the role of red herring is Andy Garcia as Jessica's partner, Mike Delmarco, himself a magnet for suspicion. Rounding out the for-the-paycheck hamfest is Samuel L. Jackson as Police Commissioner Mills, who raised Jessica after her own father (Mills' former partner) may or may not have killed himself along with her mother.

At one point in the film, Jackson, the early front-runner for this year's Best Scene-Chewing Performance, snaps at the suggestion to pull Jessica off the case, qualifying his objection by saying, "It will ruin her career." If professional humiliation is what he's worried about, forget the case; just remove her name from the opening credits.

The film opens with a moody, mist-covered shot of San Francisco Bay -- an apt metaphor for the fog of laugh-out-loud incoherence to follow. Kaufman, whose directing credentials include such critically acclaimed films as "The Right Stuff" (1983) and "The Unbearable Lightness of Being" (1988), plunges headlong into the cheesy world of made-for-TV melodrama. "Twisted" desperately tries to be sexy but can't generate enough inertia to break free of the gravitational pull of its hackneyed script. It is pulp without pop or pizzazz. Leaving no crime cliche unturned, Kaufman even has one of the police interrogators ask a frazzled Jessica, "Where were you on the night of September the 25th?"
Watching "Twisted," it is hard to keep a "straight" face.

Due to several sexual encounters with fleeting rear nudity, recurring images of crime scene gore, some brief violence, as well as frequent rough and crude language, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is L -- limited adult audience, films whose problematic content many adults would find troubling. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.
